title: Chat System: Complete Architecture
description: Design a scalable real-time chat system with monolith and microservice architectures using React, ASP.NET Core, Azure, and AWS.

data.text: Design a real-time chat system like Slack or WhatsApp that supports 1:1 direct messages, group conversations with up to 50,000 members, online presence indicators, typing indicators, read receipts, and end-to-end encryption for sensitive channels. The system must handle 100M+ concurrent WebSocket connections and 10B+ messages per day with sub-100ms delivery latency.

data.title: Functional Requirements
items: Users can send and receive text messages in real-time via WebSocket or SSE fallback
Users can create 1:1 conversations and group channels with member lists and roles
Users can see online/offline/away presence status for contacts and group members
Users see typing indicators when another user is composing a message
Messages show delivery status: sent, delivered, read (double-check marks)
Users can share images, files, and voice notes with preview generation
Offline users receive queued messages on reconnect with proper message ordering
Users can search message history by keyword within a conversation
Admins can archive, pin, and delete messages in channels they manage
Push notifications on mobile when the app is backgrounded or closed

data.title: Non-Functional Requirements
items: Sub-100ms end-to-end message delivery between two online users on the same region
99.99% message delivery rate — no silent drops; duplicates acceptable at most once
Support 100M concurrent persistent WebSocket connections across all regions
Messages maintain total causal ordering per 1:1 conversation; group chat uses per-sender ordering
Presence status updates propagate to all conversation members within 5 seconds
Offline message queue can hold 10,000 messages per user without message loss
Horizontal scalability: add hub nodes without dropping active connections
Message history is paginated with cursor-based pagination, not offset

data.text: Build a monolithic ASP.NET Core application using SignalR for real-time messaging. All chat state — connections, message history, presence, and user data — lives in a single SQL Server database. A background hosted service runs a connection map to route SignalR messages. This validates the WebSocket lifecycle, message persistence, and basic presence logic before splitting.

terms.term: - SignalR Hub (ChatHub) for real-time message routing
- Entity Framework Core with SQL Server for message history
- Background IHostedService for connection tracking and broadcast fan-out
- Azure SignalR Service sticky session via ScaleoutMode = Default
- Cloudflare R2 / Azure Blob for media message storage
- Azure App Service with ARR affinity disabled (SignalR scale-out)
- Azure SQL Database with row-level security for conversation isolation
- Azure Cache for Redis for presence and typing indicator hot state
- Azure SignalR Service (managed) for automatic hub connection scale-out

data.text: Split the monolith into five microservices. The Message Service is write-heavy — it uses a partitioned message table with conversation ID as the partition key. The Presence Service uses Redis with sub-second TTL heartbeats. The Delivery Service maintains an offline queue per user connection node. Azure SignalR Service or AWS AppSync replace self-hosted SignalR, enabling multi-instance fan-out without sticky sessions.

items: Message Service: The write path. Accepts messages via REST (HTTP fallback) or SignalR gateway events. Persists messages in PostgreSQL with conversation_id + server_timestamp as the primary sort key. Generates a client-provided UUID (client_msg_id) for idempotent deduplication on the server. Emits MessageSent events to Kafka for downstream consumers. Uses database partitioning by conversation_id for horizontal read scaling.

Presence Service: Tracks online status using Redis SET per conversation with a per-user key TTL of 30 seconds. Clients send a heartbeat via REST every 15 seconds. When a user's heartbeat TTL expires, Presence Service emits a UserWentOffline event to all conversation members via SignalR. Presence state is eventually consistent — a user may briefly show as offline during a brief network blip.

Delivery Service: Manages offline message queues partitioned by user_id. On reconnect, the client sends a last_received_message_id cursor; Delivery Service returns all messages newer than that cursor in a single batch. For group chats, the delivery fan-out is done asynchronously via a consumer group pattern to avoid slowing down the write path. Uses Sorted Sets in Redis keyed by user_id for O(log n) queue reads.

Media Service: Handles image, voice note, and file uploads. Generates multi-resolution thumbnails using ImageSharp. Returns a signed CDN URL to the sender, which is stored as the message attachment. Enforces per-user upload quotas and file-type restrictions. Publishes MediaUploaded events for content-moderation scanning via Azure Content Safety or AWS Rekognition.

User Service: Manages user profiles, avatars, contact lists, and block lists. Returns lightweight user presence snippets (name, avatar URL, online status) consumed by the Message Service to enrich message payloads before fan-out. Exposes gRPC for low-latency profile lookups during message dispatch.

- useChatConnection handles SignalR reconnect with exponential backoff (1s -> 30s max)
- Message list uses react-virtuoso for 100k+ message performance
- useOfflineQueue persists unsent messages to IndexedDB, flushes on reconnect
- Typing indicator debounces emit by 3s; stops after 5s of inactivity
- Optimistic message append with rollback on SendMessage error

data.title: SignalR Hub with Idempotent Message Ingestion

cards.title: Real-Time Hub
cards.description: Managed WebSocket pub/sub with automatic multi-instance scale-out for SignalR
pros: No sticky sessions required — SDK handles connection routing
Built-in backplane for broadcasting across hub instances
cons: Azure SignalR is opinionated; AppSync requires GraphQL schema

cards.title: Event Streaming
cards.description: Consume message events for delivery tracking, push notifications, and analytics
pros: Partitioned by conversation_id for ordered per-conversation consumption
Retention supports replay for delivery audit and compliance
cons: Consumer group coordination adds operational complexity

cards.title: Cache
cards.description: Presence heartbeats, typing indicators, and active conversation read-cursors
pros: Keyspace notifications for presence expiry events
Sub-millisecond SET/GET for typing indicator broadcast
cons: Redis Cluster mode required for >250k writes/sec

cards.title: Database
cards.description: Append-only message history partitioned by conversation_id
pros: Cosmos PostgreSQL inherits pgvector for semantic message search
DynamoDB provides single-digit ms reads at any scale
cons: Cosmos DB RU/s budgeting for unpredictable group-chat fan-out

cards.title: Push Notifications
cards.description: Background push to iOS/Android when app is backgrounded
pros: Notification Hubs handles per-platform registration and tag targeting
SNS supports SMS and mobile in addition to APNs/FCM
cons: SNS topic-per-conversation does not scale to 100M channels

data.title: When to Choose Microservices?
data.text: Start with a monolith. Split into microservices only when you have clear scaling bottlenecks, independent deployment needs, or team boundaries that justify the operational overhead.

data.title: Summary
points: Message delivery is a fan-out problem: use a managed SignalR/AppSync hub, not self-hosted WebSockets at scale
Client-generated message IDs are the simplest idempotency mechanism — deduplicate on arrival
Cursor-based pagination (not OFFSET) is mandatory for conversations with 100k+ messages
Presence must be eventually consistent — use Redis TTL heartbeats, not in-memory maps
Offline delivery requires a per-user, per-device queue; flush on reconnect using last_received_id
The write path (message ingestion) must not wait for fan-out — use an outbox + consumer group pattern
data.takeaway: Chat systems are connection-heavy, write-heavy distributed systems. Managed real-time hubs, Redis-backed presence with TTL heartbeats, an outbox pattern for durable writes, and cursor-based message pagination are the architectural pillars that separate a functional prototype from a system that handles 100M concurrent connections.
